For Marx, the state is not a neutral umpire. It is a tool of the ruling class. In capitalism, that class is the bourgeoisie, the owners of factories and capital.

"The executive of the modern state is but a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie."
The Communist Manifesto, 1848

The economic base is how a society produces things and who owns what. The superstructure is the state, law, religion and culture.

In classical Marxism, the base shapes the superstructure. Change the economy and the state changes too.

In The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State (1884), Engels argued that the state appears when society splits into classes with opposing interests.

The state did not always exist, and it will not always exist. It arose with private property.

After a revolution, workers set up a dictatorship of the proletariat to crush the old ruling class.

Once classes disappear, the state has no purpose left. It does not get abolished; it "withers away", as Engels put it in Anti-Dühring.

Lenin expanded this in The State and Revolution (1917).

Marx himself noticed that the state is not always a simple puppet. In The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, he described a situation where classes were balanced, and the state under Louis Bonaparte gained independence from all of them.

This is called Bonapartism. Later Marxists built on it to argue the state has relative autonomy.

Ralph Miliband: instrumentalist

In The State in Capitalist Society (1969), he showed that the elite running the state come from the same class and schools as the capitalists. The state is their instrument.

Nicos Poulantzas: structuralist

He replied that who sits in office does not matter, and that the state has relative autonomy from individual capitalists. The structure of capitalism forces any state to protect capital, whoever runs it.

Their exchange in New Left Review (1969–70) is a UPSC favourite.

Antonio Gramsci asked why workers in the West did not revolt. His answer was hegemony.

The ruling class rules not just by force but by consent. Schools, media and churches make the existing order look natural and common sense.

State = political society + civil society, hegemony armoured by coercion.
From the Prison Notebooks

• Economic reductionism. It reduces everything to class and neglects caste, gender, race and religion.
  • The withering never happened. The USSR built one of the strongest states in history.
  • The welfare state. Capitalist states gave workers real gains, which is hard to explain as pure class rule.
  • Pluralists argue power is spread across many groups, not held by one class.

Indian Marxists have tried to explain the Indian state. Pranab Bardhan, in The Political Economy of Development in India (1984), identified three dominant proprietary classes: industrial capitalists, rich farmers and professionals including bureaucrats. No single one rules, so the state balances them.

This mixes Marxism with Bonapartist relative autonomy, a good example to use.

"Discuss the Miliband–Poulantzas debate on the nature of the state."
"The state is an instrument of class domination." Comment.

Tip: move from Marx to Engels to Lenin, then to Gramsci, Miliband and Poulantzas. Always end with Bardhan or another Indian application.

quiz.q: "A committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie" comes from…
Who argued the instrumentalist view of the state?
quiz.w: Ralph Miliband, The State in Capitalist Society (1969).

o: State autonomy when classes are balanced
quiz.w: From Marx's Eighteenth Brumaire: the state gains autonomy when classes balance.
Hegemony: rule through consent, backed by coercion.

quiz.q: Bardhan identified how many dominant proprietary classes in India?
quiz.w: Three: industrial capitalists, rich farmers, and professionals.
